theme: Naming Our Team, Counting Our Strength
hindi: दुर्योधन द्रोणाचार्य से कहता है: “आप स्वयं, भीष्म, कर्ण, कृपाचार्य, सदा युद्ध जीतने वाले, अश्वत्थामा, विकर्ण और सोमदत्त के पुत्र भूरिश्रवा, ये सब हमारी ओर के प्रमुख वीर हैं।”
english: Duryodhana tells Drona the names of the great warriors on his side: Drona himself, Bhishma, Karna, Kripa (always victorious in battle), Ashvatthama, Vikarna, and Saumadatti, the son of Somadatta.
deeper: In this verse Duryodhana begins his list of heroes on his own side. The first name he says is “bhavān”, which means “you”. He is speaking to Drona, his teacher and commander, so he puts Drona first. It is polite, and it also shows that Duryodhana wants Drona to feel important and stay committed.

Then come Bhishma, the respected grandsire; Karna, the great archer; Kripa, who is described as samitiñjaya, “victorious in battle”; Drona’s son Ashvatthama; Duryodhana’s own brother Vikarna; and Saumadatti, the son of Somadatta. A leader who lists his strengths this way is gathering courage. Naming what we have can make us feel steadier.

But the verse also asks us to look a little deeper. A long list of famous names can sound strong, yet true strength also needs a good purpose and a calm heart. Duryodhana counts people, while Arjuna, in the next verses, will count something different: his own doubts and duty. The Gita will slowly teach us which kind of counting really matters.
background: The two armies stand ready at Kurukshetra. Blind King Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya what is happening (1.1). Seeing the Pandava army arranged for battle, Duryodhana goes to his teacher Drona and speaks (1.2). He points out the strong Pandava warriors one by one: Bhima, Arjuna, Yuyudhana, Virata, Drupada and others (1.4–1.6).

Now, in 1.7, Duryodhana turns to his own side. He says, “Now also know the chief warriors on our side, the leaders of my army. I will name them for your information.” Verse 1.8 is the start of that list, and it begins with Drona himself.
lessons: It helps to remember the good people and skills we have, especially before a big task.
Duryodhana begins with “you”, Drona. Speaking respectfully to elders is a good habit.
A team full of famous players still needs the right purpose and a clear heart.
Sometimes we talk loudly about our strength because we feel nervous inside. It is good to notice that feeling honestly.
Teamwork has many kinds of people
The list has elders, a brother, a friend and a teacher’s son. Every team is made of different relationships.
examples: Rohan is captain of the lane cricket team. He names his best bowler, best batter and best fielder before the match. It makes the whole team feel ready.
Before a school quiz, Meera thanks her teacher, Mrs. Iyer, for helping her practise. She remembers that her success has many helpers.
Before the maths test, Aarav lists the chapters he has learnt well. This calms his nervousness and shows him what still needs revision.
Kabir keeps saying, “Our team is the best!” before the kabaddi final. Later he admits he was just feeling nervous, and his friend helps him relax.
At Diwali, the whole family shares the work. Dadi plans the sweets, Papa hangs the lights, and Ananya draws the rangoli. Everyone has a part.
Sneha makes a list of who will do the costumes, music and lines for the school play. Knowing each person’s strength makes planning easier.
Famous is not the same as good
Ishaan’s group has the best-known students, but they quarrel. Another group works together happily and finishes the project first.
Tara and her younger brother Dev are on the same relay team. She cheers for him by name, and he runs faster because she believes in him.

story.title: Drona’s Test of the Wooden Bird
paras: When the Kuru princes were learning archery from Guru Drona, he once wanted to test them. He placed a wooden bird high on a tree and asked each prince to aim at it. But first he asked each one a question: “Tell me what you see.”

Yudhishthira said, “I see the tree, the branches, the bird, and you, my teacher, and my brothers.” Drona asked him to step aside. Several other princes also named many things around them, and each was asked to step aside.

Then it was Arjuna’s turn. “I see only the eye of the bird,” he said. Drona smiled. Arjuna did not count the tree, the people or the sky. His mind was steady on his aim. When Drona told him to shoot, the arrow hit the target.

On the battlefield, Duryodhana counts big names to feel strong. Drona, who taught the bird test, already knew that great names alone are not enough. A calm mind that knows what matters is also needed.
story.moral: Lesson: Counting strong names can give courage, but a steady mind and a clear purpose are what truly bring success.

quiz.q: Whom does Duryodhana name first in this verse?
o: Drona, whom he is speaking to
quiz.x: He begins with “bhavān”, meaning “you”, which refers to Drona.

quiz.q: What does “samitiñjaya” describe in this verse?
quiz.x: Samitiñjaya means “victorious in battle” and is used here for Kripa.
Ashvatthama was the son of Drona and fought on the Kaurava side.

quiz.q: What honest lesson can we take from Duryodhana’s long list?
o: Names help, but purpose and a steady mind matter more
Lists are a waste of time
quiz.x: Knowing our strengths is useful, but real strength also needs a good purpose and a calm heart.

reel.hook: Is a team full of famous names always strong?
reel.lesson: Know your strengths, but remember that purpose and a steady mind matter most.
reel.caption:
Duryodhana lists his mighty warriors, but is a long list of names enough? 🏹
Today’s Gita verse teaches us to know our strengths and keep a calm, clear heart. 🌟
